summary:
Santander is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework, whose formal provisions are among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route under which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official who defended the change described those examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Access to premises and to dignified treatment in custody rests on specific court orders. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (guards at the Cosmocentro mall in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (police at the Santa Marta boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, while a May 2018 executive decree extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence directed at trans Colombians. On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, assaulted in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon, and although police interrogated local residents no one had been arrested as of 14 April 2025. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. The incidents in Antioquia occurred outside Santander, and the hate-crime totals cover Colombia as a whole.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed groups. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that all will be military targets, including trans people. In Caquetá, "social cleansing" flyers appeared on the streets and via WhatsApp naming faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes as legitimate targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement; three armed men gave trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed, and she fled at night after hiding for a week. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. These threats and killings took place in Caquetá, outside Santander.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern Santander inherits is national rather than local. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict, and flyer campaigns in Guajira and Caquetá show armed groups operating with impunity in departments far from Santander. A visitor crossing departmental boundaries should expect the same national legal protections and the same national level of risk, without assuming that enforcement capacity varies predictably by department.

Earlier fatal attacks cited in reporting include gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and victims killed in their homes or in a hairdresser. These cases indicate that risk attaches to routine activity, dating apps, street sleeping and private premises, not only to street confrontation.

Colombia's protections are repeatedly contrasted by UN bodies with the gap between law and practice. The May 2025 UN Independent Expert's finding of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience is the clearest available comparator for what formal rights are worth on the ground.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Santander-level enforcement data, hate-crime statistics or departmental police practice guidance appears in the sources reviewed; the homicide totals cited here are national figures and the specific incidents recorded in Antioquia and Caquetá fall outside Santander. Whether the November 2025 identification markers are issued without friction at notaries in Santander itself is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The sources do not record the outcome of the investigation President Petro ordered into the April 2025 killing beyond the absence of arrests on 14 April 2025, nor whether prosecutions followed the flyer campaigns in Guajira and Caquetá. Both remain unresolved.
